extracted.intended_audience: general readers and historians of mathematics; readers interested in mathematical biography, criticism, and satire
extracted.subtask_description: A biographical/critical essay on mathematicians, mathematical ideas, and the presentation of mathematics in print; includes anecdotes, satire, and commentary on editorial and pedagogical practice. Not a formal guideline document but contains prescriptive comments about writing, editing, and teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence of alterations in published works
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever altered works are published, the fact of alteration should be made as prominent as the name of the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Everything short of this is suppression of truth, and will ultimately destroy the credit of the Society. Equally necessary is it that the alterations should be noted." Emphasises disclosure of editorial changes to preserve truth and reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and fidelity in presentation of algebra to learners
rubrics_metrics.description: If the manner in which algebra was presented to the learner had been true algebra, [critics like Frend] would have been right; confusion in presentation leads to justified protest against the subject as taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer amendment to rejection when instructing; present algebra as genuine algebra (not obscured by misleading formulation) so that objections stem from real content rather than poor pedagogy. Clear English and correct exposition are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness of algebraic signs (use of + and -)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single quantity can never be marked with either of those signs, or considered as either affirmative or negative; the affirmativeness or negativeness of any quantity implies a relation to another quantity to which it is to be added or from which it is to be subtracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present +5 or -5 standing alone as meaningful without specifying the relation; otherwise such usage is 'nonsense and unintelligible jargon.' Ensure notation is defined and used with regard to relational context (extension of terms must be explained).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match level and style to intended audience (readability and utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that attempt to be both elaborate and elementary (e.g., long heavy dissertations disguised as elementary exposition) become unreadable and unsuited to either audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid diluting little matter with much ink; ensure that scope, depth, and style align with whether the work is elementary or advanced. A mismatch (too elaborate for elementary, too elementary for higher students) makes a work unsaleable and unreadable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight given to old notes and marginalia as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Old notes, made in books by their possessors, are statements of high authority: they are almost always confirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat marginalia and owners' annotations as valuable provenance/evidence, though use with appropriate caution; they often corroborate printed accounts and can be high-quality sources for bibliographic/historical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of satire depends on audience and clarity of target
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not easy to make pungent scoffs upon what is common sense to all mankind; in an article intended for the general reader there would have been no force of satire if division by 0 had been separated from multiplication by the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When satirising mathematical ideas, ensure the target and the concepts are clearly presented and (if necessary) separated to produce comedic or critical effect; consider the audience's background knowledge so satire has force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in historical/legal terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctions of terms like 'expelled' vs 'banished' are important: people often cannot see the difference but it 'made all the difference' to the subject's status and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historically and legally precise language when reporting events; small verbal differences can materially affect a person's record and how readers perceive events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching algebra as mere rules or confusing formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebra taught 'according to certain rules and numerating formulas' may appear as a confused art which 'turbates and obscures' the mind rather than a science to be cultivated and rendered more perspicuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce algebra to rote rules without conceptual explanation; teaching should cultivate understanding and clarity rather than obscure by formulaic presentation (citations of Descartes used to illustrate the point).
